book.title: The New Penguin Book of The Guardian Crosswords, volume 2

clue.text: Account for a secret service plant

parts.note: AC is the standard short form of account, as in a/c
taken as written
the American intelligence agency

explanation.surface: Someone has to explain the presence of a spy agency's mole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a planted agent in a spy story; it is the definition, a tree or shrub.
explanation.definitionFit: The acacia is a thorny tree or shrub, the wattle of Australia, so it is one kind of vegetation.

clue.text: It's not one's own cot

definitions.meaning: first meaning: copied work, lifted from someone else

explanation.surface: A baby sleeps in a borrowed cot.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase about a borrowed bed; split it and the first part is plagiarised work, the second a baby's bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A crib is a translation or answer copied from another student, and in America also an infant's bed.

clue.text: Swelling belief about endless vista

indicators.note: without an end, so the view word loses its final letter
going around, so the creed word wraps the shortened view word

parts.note: a creed or statement of belief
a scene is a view, here cut short

explanation.surface: Faith grows around a view that seems to go on forever.
explanation.definitionFit: In music a crescendo is a gradual increase in loudness, a swelling of the sound.

clue.text: Rendering of la main or la bête?

indicators.note: rendering is a version or reworking, so the French words are reshaped

parts.note: French for the hand, used only for its letters

explanation.surface: A translator wonders how to render a French phrase: the hand, or the beast?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rendering' also means translation, and the French phrase la bête translates directly to the answer, so the clue works both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: La bête is French for the beast, and an English rendering of that is a creature or brute.

clue.text: Rumour to John Stuart of Don's giant?

parts.note: as in getting wind of something, a whisper of news
John Stuart Mill, the Victorian philosopher

explanation.surface: Gossip passed to a philosopher about a Spanish knight's imaginary enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: Don Quixote charged at what he took to be giants; they were the sails of these, which is why the definition has a question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cervantes' novel the knight attacks mills turning in the breeze, believing them to be monstrous giants.

clue.text: Poet who'd shun nude gay, what? Unlikely

indicators.note: an unlikely arrangement is not the natural one, so these letters must be rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A poet who would avoid a naked gay man? That seems improbable.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the poet was himself gay, hence 'Unlikely'. W.H. Auden's first names were Wystan Hugh.
explanation.definitionFit: W. H. Auden was the Anglo-American writer of verse such as Funeral Blues and September 1, 1939.

clue.text: Many are MPs, frank, upstanding and doing more than right by the family

definitions.text: doing more than right by the family

indicators.note: standing up in a down entry means the letters run from bottom to top

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, a great many
members of Parliament sit, as in sitting for a constituency
candid, straightforward

explanation.surface: A satirical aside: plenty of politicians are honest and upright, yet still favour their relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upstanding' looks like praise for the politicians; it turns the joined pieces upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Nepotism is favouritism shown to relatives, such as giving them jobs, which is more than their fair due.

clue.text: In ancient Rome mum's the word

definitions.text: In ancient Rome mum's the word

parts.note: surface reading: the idiom for keeping a secret, in a Roman setting

parts.words: In ancient Rome mum's the word
parts.note: setter's reading: the Latin word the Romans used for a mother

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum's the word' is an English idiom meaning keep quiet; here it literally asks what the word for mum was in Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin was the language of ancient Rome, and its noun for a mother is the source of maternal.

clue.text: Foreign articles about soldiers on hill — e.g. Moses?

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece sits on top of the next, so the hill comes last
around, so the French articles enclose the soldiers

parts.note: the French definite articles les and la
GI is an American soldier, used here as a plural
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Imported articles wrapped round troops on a hilltop, reminding someone of the man on Mount Sinai.
explanation.walkthrough: The GI goes inside the first article, LES, before the second article LA follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Moses is the lawgiver of the Bible, who brought down the Ten Commandments, so he is an example of a lawmaker.

clue.text: Wearies one as a prophet

parts.note: makes weary
the Roman numeral for one
the word as, with the article acting as a link

explanation.surface: Someone finds a soothsayer tiresome.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiresias is the blind seer of Greek myth who appears in Oedipus and The Waste Land.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiresias was the blind Theban seer of Greek legend, who foretold Oedipus's fate.

clue.text: Writer gets label in the soup

indicators.note: the writer receives something into himself, holding it inside

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe, the American author
a tag is a label attached to something

explanation.surface: An author ends up labelled as being in trouble, in the soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the soup' looks like the idiom for trouble; the soup itself is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Potage is a thick French-style soup, from the old word pottage.

clue.text: Typify carter travelling in open carriage

indicators.note: inside, so the shuffled letters sit within the vehicle

parts.note: a chaise is a light, often open, horse-drawn carriage

indicators.note: something travelling moves around, so the driver's letters shift

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A carter riding in an open carriage is a typical sight.
explanation.definitionFit: To characterise something is to be typical of it or mark its distinctive qualities.

clue.text: River dividing public transport route gives added bounce

definitions.note: describes what the thing does rather than naming it

indicators.note: splitting something apart, so the river sits between the two halves of the route

parts.note: the rails a tram runs along
the Po is Italy's longest river

explanation.surface: A river cuts across a tram route.
explanation.definitionFit: A trampoline is a sprung canvas frame that throws a jumper higher, adding spring to each leap.

clue.text: Amused expression of trapped king

indicators.note: caught in a snare, so the monarch is held inside the snare word

parts.note: a gin is a snare for catching animals
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A captured monarch manages a wry smile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trapped' does double duty: it names the gin, an old word for an animal trap, and says the king is inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A grin is a broad smile, the face someone pulls when entertained.

clue.text: 'Hot-Lips' (a MASH nurse) works here

indicators.note: works as in a set of workings, so the named letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: the nickname of Margaret Houlihan in the TV series M*A*S*H
taken as written

explanation.surface: Major Houlihan, nicknamed Hot Lips in M*A*S*H, has her workplace.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: MASH stands for Mobile Army Surgical Hospital, so Hot Lips really does work in one.
explanation.definitionFit: M*A*S*H was set in a mobile army surgical unit in Korea, where nurse Houlihan treated wounded soldiers.

clue.text: Fascinate someone in hearing of your cholesterol intake

indicators.note: as heard by a listener, so the phrase is judged by its sound

parts.note: describing a diet: the fat you have eaten

explanation.surface: A doctor talks about how much cholesterol a patient consumes.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken quickly, the phrase about fat consumption sounds like the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To infatuate is to inspire a foolish, intense passion in someone, captivating them.

clue.text: Scandal of Princess's late Princess

parts.note: Di's, belonging to Diana, Princess of Wales
Grace Kelly, Princess of Monaco, who died in 1982

explanation.surface: Gossip about one royal woman's dead royal relative.
explanation.definitionFit: A disgrace is a shameful matter, the kind of event that causes public outrage and loss of honour.

clue.text: Impressive post offices introduced to a Chinese dynasty

parts.note: a means one, and one is I

indicators.note: brought into the dynasty, so the offices go inside its name

parts.note: the Ming ruled China from 1368 to 1644
PO is the abbreviation for post office, here plural

explanation.surface: Grand postal buildings arrive in imperial China.
explanation.definitionFit: Something imposing is grand in size or manner, making a strong impression on onlookers.

clue.text: Whip that can turn into a sort of club

indicators.note: turning round means reading the letters the other way

parts.note: a golf club is one sort of club

explanation.surface: A whip that can somehow be converted into a club.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs backwards to usual: the answer, turned round, becomes the sport whose club is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: To flog is to beat with a whip or rod as punishment.

clue.text: Dark Lady loses her head on the way out

indicators.note: losing the head means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: a dated term for a Black woman, now considered offensive

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's mysterious Dark Lady is beheaded on her way out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dark Lady' evokes Shakespeare's sonnets; the wordplay uses an old, now offensive word.
explanation.definitionFit: An egress is an exit, a route by which one leaves a place.

clue.text: Sentimental pitch to attain tricky goal

parts.note: touching, emotionally stirring
pitch is a black tarry substance
to get something is to attain it

explanation.surface: An emotional sales pitch aimed at reaching a hard objective.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' looks like a sales pitch; it is the sticky black substance.
explanation.definitionFit: A moving target is a goal that keeps shifting, so it is difficult to reach or hit.

clue.text: Sugary film made from an epic in Greek

indicators.note: made out of the following words, which hold the letters inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A sweet movie adapted from a Greek epic, like the Iliad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' suggests a movie; it is a thin coating.
explanation.definitionFit: Icing is the thin sweet coating spread over cakes, a layer or skin of sugar.

clue.text: City which features in shipbuilding

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the port city in Yorkshire, England
second meaning: the body of a ship

explanation.surface: A city known for building ships.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull, on the Humber estuary in Yorkshire, is a port city with a shipping history, so the surface rings true.
explanation.definitionFit: The hull is the main body or shell of a vessel, built first in any shipyard.

clue.text: After thirty seconds, poor aim yields lowest points

indicators.note: a poor shot is badly made, so these letters are set wrong

parts.note: thirty seconds is half a minute, and half of minute as a word is its first three letters
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: After half a minute of bad shooting, the scores are at their lowest.
explanation.walkthrough: Half a minute is taken literally: half the word minute.
explanation.definitionFit: Minima is the Latin plural of minimum, the smallest values or troughs on a graph.

clue.text: Early flier, late back, gets left in Australia

indicators.note: the first piece acquires the next one, joining it on
going back means the word is read from end to start

parts.note: the late someone is someone who has died

indicators.note: inside, so the letter for left sits within the country

parts.note: the country's abbreviation
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A pioneering aviator returns late and is stranded down under.
explanation.walkthrough: Daedalus in Greek myth made wings of feathers and wax for himself and his son Icarus.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Daedalus escaped Crete on wings he built, so he was among the first to fly.

clue.text: Settle in to write of boat's shade in Lear?

indicators.note: settle goes inside the writing word

parts.note: to pen something is to write it
to settle on terms is to agree

explanation.surface: A writer prepares to describe the colour of a boat in a Lear poem.
explanation.walkthrough: In Edward Lear's poem, the Owl and the Pussy-cat went to sea in a beautiful boat of this colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Lear's nonsense poem describes the vessel as a beautiful pea-green boat, so this is its colour.

clue.text: Brownshirts swallow their greeting to a girl

indicators.note: swallowing takes something inside, so the greeting goes within

parts.note: the Sturmabteilung, the Nazi stormtroopers known as Brownshirts
the Nazi salute word, German for hail

explanation.surface: Stormtroopers give their salute to a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheila is Australian slang for a woman or girl.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian and New Zealand slang a sheila is a young woman or girl.
